intro: La Salle is a village in the upper Aosta Valley, on the road from Aosta towards Courmayeur and Mont Blanc. Above it a path climbs through larch and spruce towards the Col du Bard, and beside that path a reader found an old larch with a broad, leaning trunk and limbs hung all over with beard lichen. They sent us its photograph and a note urging others to go and see it.
meta_description: An old, lichen-hung European larch beside the path to the Col du Bard above La Salle, Aosta Valley, sent by a reader.

trees.name: The Bearded Larch of the Col du Bard Path
trees.age_estimate: more than 500 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Mountain path from Challancin towards the Col du Bard, La Salle, Aosta Valley

trees.story:
On the climb from La Salle towards the Col du Bard, high in the Aosta Valley, a reader stopped beside this larch and sent us its photograph. "The energy near of him it's simply magic and majestic," they wrote. "I advise to go to see him!"

The picture shows why. The trunk is broad and dark, deeply furrowed and swollen on one side, and it leans a little over the path as if it has been listening to walkers for a long time. Its limbs do not reach up so much as pour down, long and crooked, some of them almost touching the ground, and every one is hung with grey-green beard lichen, the kind that only grows in clean mountain air. Younger larches and spruces stand around it; none of them comes close.

The reader puts it at more than 500 years old and its trunk at about four metres round. Those figures are theirs; we have not seen a measurement or a record of this tree. They describe the path as signed, and a small wooden marker stands on it just past the trunk. Further up, they say, the views open onto Mont Blanc, the Grivola and the Gran Paradiso.

Come in October, when the larches of the valley turn gold.
trees.how_to_recognise: Beside the mountain path, just below a small wooden signpost: a broad, leaning larch trunk, swollen on one side, its long crooked limbs sweeping down almost to the ground and hung all over with grey-green beard lichen.
trees.access: Free. It stands beside a public mountain path above La Salle, on the way up to the Col du Bard; a walk uphill, not a stroll.

A second frame: the same larch from further down the path, the trail running up past its foot to the little signpost, the lichen-hung limbs and a younger larch beside it, overcast daylight, colour. No register entry within 100 m, no encyclopaedia article within 300 m (corroborate.py); the MASAF register's La Salle entry is a chestnut at Derby, not this tree. question_meta: An old, lichen-hung European larch beside the path to the Col du Bard above La Salle, Aosta Valley, sent by a reader.
question_answer: The Bearded Larch of the Col du Bard Path stands beside the mountain path that climbs from Challancin, above La Salle in the Aosta Valley, towards the Col du Bard. It is free to see from the path.
question_context: A reader walking up from La Salle towards the Col du Bard, in the upper Aosta Valley, stopped beside this European larch and sent us its photograph with a note calling the feeling near it simply magic and majestic. The picture bears them out. The trunk is broad, dark and deeply furrowed, swollen on one side and leaning a little over the path, and its long crooked limbs sweep down almost to the ground, every one hung with grey-green beard lichen. Younger larches and spruces stand around it, and a small wooden signpost marks the path just past its foot. The reader puts it at more than 500 years old and its trunk at about four metres round; those figures are theirs, not a measurement we have seen. Further up the same walk, they say, the views open onto Mont Blanc, the Grivola and the Gran Paradiso. The larch is the one conifer of the Alps that drops its needles each winter, so in October the whole slope turns gold.

faq.q: Can I visit The Bearded Larch of the Col du Bard Path?
faq.a: Yes. It stands beside a public mountain path above La Salle, on the way to the Col du Bard, free to walk. It is an uphill walk, so wear boots.
Look for a broad, leaning larch trunk just below a small wooden signpost, its long limbs sweeping down to the ground and hung with grey-green beard lichen.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Summer for the walk, and October, when the larches of the valley turn gold before they drop their needles.
